series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.4 · October 2026
title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment

slides.title: Credit the Price Signal, Not the Payment
slides.subtitle: Carbon price recognition and scrap shuffling under the EU's CBAM
slides.message: The EU's border charge measures carbon plant by plant and credits only carbon prices paid. Exporters can route clean steel to Europe, and a feebate earns nothing. Measure by country and sector, and credit the exporting country's price signal.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: The EU now charges steel imports hundreds of euros a tonne for their carbon

stats.label: per tonne of hot-rolled steel from India (default 4.28 tCO₂/t plus 30% mark-up)

slides.text: At €80 per tonne of CO₂ and full phase-in. The charge falls only by a carbon price "effectively paid" abroad, net of "any rebate or other form of compensation" (Art. 9(1)).
slides.source: Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 (default values); Regulation (EU) 2025/2083; working paper 1.4, Table 3.

slides.title: Measuring plant by plant pays exporters to route clean steel to Europe
slides.caption: Stylized exporter: 10 Mt a year, 2 Mt from scrap, 1 Mt sold to the EU at €80/tCO₂. Shipping only scrap-based steel to the EU cuts the carbon the border sees by 76% and the bill by €102m a year; emissions stay at 16.8 MtCO₂. Scrap is limited, so the cut is mostly relabeling.
slides.source: Author's calculation; working paper 1.4, Figure 1; IEA (2020).

slides.title: Routing is worth almost as much as the charge itself
slides.note: Across thirteen exporters the gain is €98–626 a tonne. None of it is a fall in emissions. The law asks for reports on "resource shuffling" but gives no tool to stop it.
slides.source: EU default values (Reg. 2025/2621); scrap-based steel at 0.4 tCO₂/t (stylized). Working paper 1.4, Table 3; Reg. 2023/956, Art. 30.

slides.title: A feebate gives the full carbon price at the margin, yet earns no credit

points.text: A feebate charges above the sector average and rebates below it: every producer faces the full price on each tonne it cuts; the average producer pays nothing.

points.lead: The draft rules net out the rebate.
points.text: Emissions "below an emission intensity baseline" count as compensation, so recognition is zero. A tax at the same rate would earn it all.

points.lead: The default carbon price covers explicit prices only.
points.text: From 2027, only "where a carbon price was set by the rules"; the method being prepared starts from carbon taxes and trading systems.

slides.source: Draft implementing regulation Ares(2026)4841230, Art. 8(1)(b)(ii); Reg. 2025/2083, Art. 9(4); Technopolis (2026).

slides.title: One value per country and sector ends shuffling, but leaves each plant almost no incentive

points.lead: No plant can choose what the border sees,
points.text: so routing and picking defaults earn nothing.

points.lead: But a clean plant lowers the average for everyone.
points.text: If a tenth of output goes to the EU, the country gains €8 per tonne of CO₂ cut; a mill with a tenth of the country's output keeps €0.80.

points.lead: A value fixed for years gives no incentive at all.
points.text: It must be the verified sector average, updated yearly.

points.lead: Standardized values have the same gap:
points.text: Neuhoff et al. (2026) note they create no direct incentive abroad.

slides.source: Working paper 1.4, Proposition 3; Neuhoff et al. (2026).

slides.title: Crediting the country's price signal restores the incentive on every tonne

points.text: importers pay the EU price less a recognized foreign price, on the country-sector average carbon content. The recognized price is the price paid plus a weight on the unpaid part of the signal.
and a feebate at the EU price stays the exporter's lowest-cost choice.

points.lead: A feebate at €80 gives every plant €80 a tonne
points.text: on all its output, not only the tenth sold in Europe.
as a carbon-price equivalent (Brief 6.1): tax, feebate, subsidy reform, standard.

slides.source: Working paper 1.4, Proposition 5; Mehling and Ritz (2023) for explicit prices only.

slides.title: With recognition, a feebate at the EU price pays off at a quarter of output sold to the EU, not half
slides.source: Author's calculation, stylized abatement costs; working paper 1.4, Figure 3.
slides.caption: Selling a tenth of output to the EU, a country's own best feebate rises from €8 to €21 with full recognition (A). A feebate at €80 breaks even at 50% of output sold to the EU today, 24% with recognition (B). Stylized abatement costs.

slides.title: Phase recognition in with the end of free allocation, and keep verification where there is no signal

points.text: a feebate country's steel could enter without a carbon charge while EU steel pays on all its emissions.

points.lead: So tie recognition to free allocation:
points.text: weight = 1 − CBAM factor: 2.5% in 2026, about half in 2030, full from 2034 (or 2038 if extended). Review relocation at each step.
firms verify the whole output of all their plants.
mark-up and support test by implementing act; crediting the signal needs Article 9 amended.

slides.source: Directive (EU) 2023/959, Art. 10a(1a); COM(2026) 616; working paper 1.4, Sections on design and legal pathway.
